title: Haul water without wrecking your back: drum roller, cart, yoke or sled
summary: A litre of water weighs about a kilogram, so one 20 L jerry can is 20 kg, and a family of four at Canada's emergency-kit figure of four litres a person a day needs about 16 kg a day, over 100 kg a week. Roll it, pull it or push it instead of carrying it: a drum clamped between two plywood wheels (our own design: no source has tested it), a cart or bike trailer, a sled on snow, or a yoke for short trips. The dangers are backs, falls on ice, and getting wet and cold on the way.

materials.item: Food-grade plastic drum with a screw cap that seals, up to about 90 litres (the Hippo Roller's size)
Plywood, 18 mm (3/4 in) or thicker, for two disc wheels a few centimetres bigger than the drum's ends
Threaded rod or long bolts, 10–12 mm, with nuts and big washers, to clamp the discs to the drum
Two short bolts for stub axles, with lock nuts and washers
Steel tube, conduit or straight timber for a U-shaped handle
Rope or webbing for a pull harness and for lashing
Jerry cans or jugs with tight lids, 10–20 litres each
Sled or toboggan for snow, or a cart, wagon or bike trailer for roads
Ice grippers or cleats for your boots
Cooler or insulated box to stop jugs freezing on a long cold haul

steps.text: Work out the weight before you plan the trip. Water is about 1 gram per millilitre (USGS water density), so every litre is about a kilogram: a 20 L jerry can is 20 kg (44 lb) and a 90 L drum is 90 kg.

Pick the way to move it: carry short distances in two balanced containers or on a yoke, pull a sled on snow, and roll or push a cart or drum roller on paths and roads. CCOHS says pulling is easier than carrying, and pushing is easier than pulling (CCOHS back injury).

For the drum roller (our own design; no source has tested it, so treat your first one as a trial), check the drum: food-grade, no cracks, and a screw cap that seals when you lie it on its side full of water.
steps.warn: Don't use a drum that held toxic chemicals such as bleach or pesticides, or fuel or solvent, for drinking water (CDC water supply). If you can't tell what it held, keep it for wash and flush water.

steps.text: Draw round the drum's end on plywood, then draw a second circle a few centimetres bigger. Cut two discs on the bigger line: these are the wheels, so the drum itself never touches the ground.
On the inside face of each disc, screw a ring of short blocks round the smaller line, so the drum's end sits snugly inside it and can't slide off centre.

Drill the exact centre of each disc and fit a bolt pointing outwards as a stub axle, with big washers on both faces and a lock nut. Leave enough thread sticking out to carry the handle arm and a second lock nut.

Stand the drum between the discs. Join the discs with four threaded rods running along the outside of the drum, evenly spaced and inside the edge of the discs, and tighten them in turn until the discs grip the drum's ends firmly.
steps.warn: The rods must sit inside the disc's edge, or they will hit the ground and jam as it rolls.

steps.text: Make a U-shaped handle: two arms as long as from the axle to your hip, joined by a cross-bar to push or pull. Drill each arm's end to fit over a stub axle, and hold it with a washer and a lock nut that lets it turn freely.
steps.warn: File sharp tube ends and drilled edges smooth.

steps.text: Test it a quarter full on flat ground. Check the drum doesn't slip in its discs, the rods don't touch the ground, and the nuts stay tight. Then try it half full on the steepest slope you'll use.

Before the drum or jugs carry drinking water, wash them with soap and rinse well, then sanitise them with 1 teaspoon of unscented household bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite) in 1 quart (about 1 litre) of water: cover and shake it so it touches every surface, wait at least 30 seconds, pour it out and let them air-dry (CDC water supply). Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other cleaners: it gives off toxic gas (Health Canada chemicals). Water from a lake, river or melted snow still has to be treated before anyone drinks it: see [water in winter](#guides/skill_water_in_winter).
Fill it only to a weight you can stop and hold on the steepest part of your route, not to the brim. Hippo's roller carries 90 litres (Hippo Roller), but that is a lot to hold back downhill.
steps.warn: Never stand or walk downhill of a loaded roller, cart or sled: if it gets away it runs you down. Take slopes slowly with a rigid handle or poles holding it back, or take less water or another route.

steps.text: For a sled, lash the jugs low and flat on the sled, lids up and tight, and pull from a harness you can slip out of quickly, so your hands stay free for balance. On downhills, walk beside it, or use stiff poles or a rigid bar instead of a rope: skiers who tow sleds report that a rope lets the sled run into the backs of their knees on descents (WildSnow sled). Poles are our own suggestion here and only anecdotally tested.

On ice and packed snow, wear grippers, take short slow steps with your toes pointed slightly out, and keep your hands out of your pockets (Alberta winter walking, Manitoba icy surfaces). Spread sand or grit on paths you use every day (Manitoba icy surfaces).
steps.warn: Never haul water across lake or river ice you haven't measured, and never alone. The [thin-ice card](#browse/hazards/cold_water) gives 15 cm of clear, hard ice as the minimum on foot in a small group; white ice is about half as strong. See [water through ice](#guides/skill_water_through_ice).

steps.text: Dress for work, not standing: shed a layer before you sweat, wear waterproof mitts for filling, and take warm-up breaks. Sweat in the layer next to your skin cuts its warmth dramatically (CCOHS cold work).
steps.warn: Wet clothes on the way home are how hypothermia starts. Keep a dry layer in a bag and change into it if you get soaked ([cold](#browse/hazards/cold)).

steps.text: Lift full containers with your knees bent and the load close, without twisting (CCOHS back injury). Carry with both hands, or switch hands often (Cal/OSHA carrying).

notes:
## How heavy water is
Water is about 1 gram per millilitre (USGS water density): 1 litre is about 1 kg (2.2 lb), 20 litres about 20 kg (44 lb), 200 litres about 200 kg. Canada's emergency-kit guidance is about four litres a person a day for drinking, cooking and sanitation (Get Prepared emergency kits), so a family of four needs about 16 kg a day and over 100 kg a week, and more once you wash, flush or nurse someone sick. Plan the containers and the route before the water runs out.

| Load | Weight | Move it by |
|---|---|---|
| 10 L jug | about 10 kg | Hand, one in each hand |
| 20 L jerry can | about 20 kg | Two hands, a yoke, or wheels |
| 2–4 jerry cans | 40–80 kg | Sled, cart, wagon or bike trailer |
| 90 L drum | about 90 kg | Drum roller on a flat route |

## Why backs and necks pay
A survey in South Africa, Ghana and Vietnam found more hand and upper-back pain in people who carried water, and a pattern of pain the authors linked to squeezing the spine (head, upper back, chest and more) that was stronger in those who carried it on their heads. The authors suggest wheelbarrows and better paths as alternatives where water can't be piped to the house (Geere 2018). It was a survey, so it shows a link, not proof.

CCOHS's advice for any lifting job applies here (CCOHS back injury):
- Make loads lighter: split the water into two or more containers.
- Pull rather than carry, and push rather than pull. Yokes and trucks are on its list of handling aids.
- Keep the load close to your body; don't twist or bend sideways while lifting.
- Lowering is easier than lifting, so keep the full containers at the height you'll use them.
- Use rest breaks, so tiredness doesn't build up.
See also [lifting heavy things](#guides/safety_lifting).

How much is too much: CCOHS gives NIOSH's 23 kg (51 lb) as a load that is safe for 75% of women and 90% of men only under ideal conditions, which on that page means two-handed lifts, comfortable postures, a comfortable environment and non-slip floors (CCOHS NIOSH). Ice, cold, a bent back at a hole and a can held at arm's length are not ideal, so a full 20 L can is already near the limit. Use 10 L jugs for hand carrying on ice, and let wheels or a sled take the rest.

## Which carrier
| Carrier | Best on | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| Two jugs, or a yoke | Short trips, steps, rough ground | Keep both sides about equal. Use both hands, and swap hands often if you carry one (Cal/OSHA carrying) |
| Sled or toboggan | Snow and packed trails | Runs into your legs downhill; tips on side slopes |
| Cart, wagon, wheelbarrow | Roads, paths, hard snow | Load over the axle; see [hand cart](#guides/build_hand_cart) |
| Bike trailer | Roads, longer trips | The trailer's rated load on its label; brake early |
| Drum roller | Flat paths, dry ground | Hard to stop downhill; sinks in soft snow |

A yoke is a padded pole across the shoulders with a container hanging from each end. Keep the two sides equal and the cords short, so the loads don't swing into your legs.

## About the drum roller
The Hippo Roller is a 90-litre rolling drum, made to spare people carrying 25-litre buckets several times a day (Hippo Roller). The version here is our own design, not a copy of the Hippo Roller, and no source has tested it. It clamps a salvaged drum between two plywood wheels with rods along the outside, so nothing goes through the drum, and the water touches only the drum's plastic if the drum is food-grade. Treat your first one as a trial: start with a small load, and check for the drum slipping, cracks in the drum or discs, and loose nuts before every trip. A wooden cable reel from a building site has the same two-discs-and-a-barrel shape and might supply the discs if the wood is sound; that is untested too. If anything shifts, go back to a cart or sled.

A poly lawn roller from a garden centre or hardware store is a ready-made rolling drum with a push or tow handle: Agri-Fab's 46 × 61 cm (18 × 24 in) roller fills from a garden hose through a drain plug and is rated at 250 lb (about 113 kg) (Agri-Fab roller). Nothing on its page says it is food-grade, so use it for washing and flushing water.

## Containers
The CDC asks for sturdy food-grade containers with tight lids, ideally with a narrow opening for pouring, and never ones that held toxic chemicals (CDC water supply). Lids keep the water clean on the way and keep it off your clothes. Mark containers for drinking water and keep them apart from ones used for wash water.

## Ice, snow and cold on the way
- Slips: Alberta Health Services says to walk slowly with small steps, toes pointed slightly out, head up, hands out of pockets, and to use grippers or cleats outdoors and take them off inside. It also warns against carrying heavy or bulky loads that upset your balance or block your view, which is one more reason to pull a sled instead (Alberta winter walking). A construction-industry safety talk (Manitoba Heavy Construction Association, hosted on a Manitoba government site) adds: keep your centre of balance under you, avoid carrying heavy loads on ice, use handrails, and spread sand or grit on paths you use often (Manitoba icy surfaces).
- Cold: hauling is hard work, and sweat soaks the layer next to your skin and kills its warmth. Wear layers you can open, a waterproof outer layer for wet work, and mittens below −17 °C. Work with a partner, take warm-up breaks, and haul in the warmer part of the day (CCOHS cold work). Insulate metal handles (CCOHS cold work). See the [cold card](#browse/hazards/cold).
- Freezing water: ice is about 9 % less dense than water (USGS water density), so a jug filled to the brim can split if it freezes. Leave room, and keep jugs in a cooler or wrapped in a sleeping pad on a long cold haul.
- Ice on lakes and rivers: see [water through ice](#guides/skill_water_through_ice) and the [thin-ice card](#browse/hazards/cold_water).

## When to leave it
A route with a long steep hill, sheet ice or deep fresh snow can make a full roller or cart more dangerous than useful. Take less, make more trips, or wait for the trail to firm up. Better still, haul less: melt snow close to home ([water in winter](#guides/skill_water_in_winter)), and set up [rainwater collection](#guides/build_rainwater_collection) for the thaw.
